name: Tetracycline stain bleaching

lead: Tetracycline staining is a deep yellow-grey-brown discolouration inside the tooth, caused by antibiotics taken during tooth development. People use extended overnight tray bleaching to lighten it for a brighter, more even smile.

Tetracycline and minocycline bind calcium and are incorporated into developing teeth, producing yellow-green staining that fluoresces under UV light and later turns brown. Peroxide gel releases reactive species that break down pigment molecules, and reference sources say tetracycline stain takes longer because the bleach must reach the dentine. Veneers or crowns are listed as alternatives for masking intrinsic stains.

paras: People wear custom-fitted trays with peroxide gel overnight, usually over weeks or months, under dental guidance. Progress is gradual, and some follow bleaching with veneers or crowns if the shade is not where they want it.
Sensitivity, gum irritation or burns from poorly fitting trays, uneven results and rebound are reported. Concentration limits are set by regulators.

angle.text: People with tetracycline-stained teeth use weeks or months of overnight peroxide tray bleaching to lighten deep yellow-grey-brown discolouration that resists normal whitening. The gel works its way into the dentine and breaks down pigment gradually. The goal is a more even, brighter smile.

lead: Tetracycline stain bleaching is the use of extended peroxide bleaching, often worn overnight over weeks or months, to lighten the intrinsic yellow-grey-brown discolouration caused by tetracycline antibiotics taken during tooth development.[1][2]

Tetracycline and minocycline bind calcium and are incorporated into developing teeth, producing yellow-green staining that fluoresces under UV light and later turns brown.[1][2] Because the stain is in the dentine, reference sources say it often needs prolonged bleaching, and they list veneers or crowns as alternatives for masking intrinsic stains.[1][2]
infobox: Prolonged; source gives no fixed period

paras: Home bleaching uses trays holding carbamide peroxide gel worn overnight or for two to four hours a day.[1] Tetracycline staining is intrinsic, and intrinsic stains generally require bleaching rather than cleaning.[2]

Reported effects of bleaching include tooth sensitivity, gum irritation, uneven results and rebound toward the original shade as teeth rehydrate.[1] Hydrogen peroxide at 10% or higher can burn soft tissue, and poorly fitting trays are a common cause of chemical burns.[1] The US FDA endorses gels containing under 6% hydrogen peroxide or up to 16% carbamide peroxide, and EU retail products are limited to 0.1% hydrogen peroxide.[1]

No studies found in the sources reviewed here that test extended bleaching on tetracycline stains specifically. A 2018 Cochrane review of home-based bleaching is cited in the general bleaching literature.[1]
